Shebang
What does the first line #!/usr/bin/env bash in a script do?
Selects the interpreter that runs the script
Marks the line as a comment that is ignored completely
Grants the script permission to run as root
Loads environment variables from the user's profile
The shebang tells the kernel which interpreter to use; env finds bash on the PATH.
m
Parameters
In a bash script, what does $1 contain?
The first command-line argument
The script's own file name
The exit status of the last command
The number of arguments passed
$0 is the script name, $1 the first argument, $# the count and $? the last exit status.
m
Exit codes
What does an exit status of 0 mean by convention?
Success
A general error occurred
The command was not found
The process was killed
0 means success; any non-zero value signals failure. 127 commonly means command not found.
d
Exit codes
A command run in a script returns exit status 126. What is the most likely cause?
The file exists but is not executable
The command was not found on the PATH
The command was terminated by SIGKILL
The command completed with a warning
126 means found but not executable (for example, missing execute permission); 127 means not found; 128+n means killed by signal n.
m
Conditions
Which test checks whether /etc/app.conf exists and is a regular file?
[ -f /etc/app.conf ]
[ -d /etc/app.conf ]
[ -z /etc/app.conf ]
[ -x /etc/app.conf ]
-f tests for a regular file; -d is a directory, -z an empty string and -x executable.
m
Loops
Which loop safely processes each line of hosts.txt, including lines with spaces?
while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < hosts.txt
for line in $(cat hosts.txt); do ...; done
for line in hosts.txt; do ...; done
until read hosts.txt; do ...; done
A while-read loop handles lines intact; for over $(cat) splits on whitespace.
d
Functions
Why should variables inside a bash function be declared with local?
To avoid overwriting variables of the same name elsewhere in the script
Because functions cannot read any variable that is not local
Because local variables are stored encrypted in memory
Because bash runs functions only when every variable is local
Bash variables are global by default; local limits their scope to the function.
d
Strict mode
What does set -u add to a script's safety?
It stops the script when an unset variable is used
It stops the script when any command prints to standard error
It prevents the script from being run by unprivileged users
It forces every variable to be written in uppercase
set -u turns references to unset variables into errors, which catches typos such as $DIRR.
d
Word splitting
Why does ShellCheck warn about unquoted variables such as cp $src $dst?
Values with spaces or glob characters split into several arguments
Unquoted variables are always empty when passed to external commands
cp refuses arguments that come from variables unless they are quoted
Unquoted variables are executed as separate commands by the shell
Quoting prevents word splitting and globbing, which otherwise change how many arguments a command receives.
m
Validating input
A script takes a username argument and passes it to userdel. What is a sensible first check?
Reject values that do not match an expected pattern
Run userdel first and check whether it reports an error
Convert the argument to uppercase before using it
Pass the argument through eval to expand any variables
Validate input against an allow-list pattern before using it. eval on user input is dangerous.
d
Secrets in scripts
Why should a backup script not contain a database password in plain text?
Anyone who can read the script or its copies obtains the credential
Bash cannot pass passwords to commands that run in the background
Plain-text passwords make the script run more slowly
Passwords in scripts expire after the script is run once
Scripts are copied, versioned and read. Use a protected credentials file, a secrets manager or the tool's own credential store.
m
Logging from scripts
Which command sends a message from a script to the system log?
logger
echo -syslog
printf --journal
write root
logger writes to syslog/journald, giving scripts a central, timestamped record.
m
Debugging
What does running a script with bash -x show?
Each command as it is executed, after expansion
Only the commands that returned an error
The script's source with comments removed
The memory used by each line of the script
-x traces expanded commands, which shows exactly what the shell runs.
d
Dry runs
Why add a --dry-run option to a script that deletes old files?
So operators can see what would be removed before anything is deleted
So the script runs faster by skipping the file-system checks
So that the deleted files can be restored after the script ends
So the script can run without the permissions it would normally need
A dry run prints intended actions without making changes, which is essential for destructive automation.
m
ShellCheck
What is ShellCheck?
A static analyser that finds common bugs in shell scripts
A service that checks whether shells are running on a server
A tool that encrypts scripts before they are deployed
A replacement shell that runs scripts in a sandbox
ShellCheck reads scripts without running them and flags issues such as unquoted variables.
m
cron format
What schedule does the cron expression 30 2 * * 1 describe?
02:30 every Monday
Every 30 minutes on day 2
02:30 on the first of each month
Every 2 hours, 30 times a week
Fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week; 1 is Monday.
d
cron environment
A command works in an interactive shell but fails from cron. What is a common reason?
cron runs with a minimal environment and PATH
cron runs every job with root privileges
cron cannot run scripts written for bash
cron jobs are blocked until a user logs in
Use absolute paths and set needed variables in the job, because cron does not load the user's profile.
d
cron security
Why is a cron job run by root that executes a script writable by other users dangerous?
Anyone who can edit the script gets their code run as root
cron will refuse to run it and stop all other scheduled jobs
The script will be deleted at the next scheduled run
It makes the system clock drift on every execution
Scheduled tasks are a well-known persistence and escalation route. Scripts run by root must be root-owned and not writable by others.
m
cron access control
Which files decide which users may create their own crontabs?
/etc/cron.allow and /etc/cron.deny
/etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
/etc/sudoers and /etc/group
/etc/hosts.allow and /etc/hosts.deny
cron.allow (if present) lists permitted users; otherwise cron.deny lists those refused.
d
systemd timers
What does Persistent=true do in a systemd timer?
Runs a missed job at the next boot if the system was off when it was due
Keeps the timer's output in memory after the job has finished
Prevents anyone from disabling the timer, including root
Makes the job restart forever if it exits with an error
Persistent timers catch up on runs missed while the machine was powered off, unlike classic cron.
m
Auditing schedules
Which command lists active systemd timers and their next run times?
systemctl list-timers
crontab -l --systemd
journalctl --timers
atq -systemd
list-timers shows each timer, its last and next trigger and the unit it activates.
m
Load average
On a 4-core server, what does a sustained load average of 8 suggest?
More work is waiting than the cores can run
The server is using 8% of its CPU
Eight users are logged in at once
The disk is 8 times faster than needed
Load counts runnable (and uninterruptible) tasks; consistently above the core count indicates saturation.
d
vmstat
vmstat shows high values in the si and so columns. What does this indicate?
The system is swapping memory to and from disk
The CPU is spending most of its time idle
Network traffic is being dropped by the kernel
Disk space on the root volume is almost full
si/so are swap-in and swap-out. Sustained swapping signals memory pressure and slows the system.
d
Alerting
Why should a disk-space alert fire at a threshold such as 85% rather than at 100%?
It gives time to act before services fail
Disks stop accepting reads above 85% full
Monitoring tools cannot measure above 85%
Thresholds below 100% reduce disk wear
Alerts must leave time to respond. At 100%, logging and databases may already have failed.
m
Disk monitoring
Which command shows free space per mounted file system in human-readable units?
df -h
du -s
ls -lh
free -h
df reports per-file-system usage; free shows memory, and du sums directory sizes.
d
Atomic writes
Why do robust scripts write output to a temporary file and then mv it into place?
The rename is atomic, so readers never see a half-written file
mv compresses files, so the final copy uses less disk space
Temporary files are automatically backed up by the system
Writing directly to the final file needs root privileges
Renaming within one file system is atomic, so consumers see either the old or the complete new file.
